title: Quality Engineering
blurb: Build confidence with tests that catch real bugs, rather than just making coverage numbers look good.

mustKnow.title: Test pyramid: when to change the balance
mustKnow.body: The test pyramid described by Mike Cohn puts many fast, focused unit tests at the base, integration tests in the middle, and a few slower, more brittle E2E tests at the top for important flows. These proportions are not fixed: when most code connects to a database or service, integration failures may deserve more emphasis, as in Kent C. Dodds’s testing trophy. Test each risk at the lowest layer that can actually detect it. Avoid an inverted pyramid, or ice-cream cone, dominated by E2E or manual tests.

mustKnow.title: Good unit tests: AAA and one behavior
mustKnow.body: Structure a test as Arrange (prepare data), Act (call the code under test), and Assert (check the result). Have each test check one behavior, with a name that states the condition and expected result so a failure immediately identifies what broke. One behavior can require several assertions, such as checking multiple fields of one returned object. Tests must run independently, without relying on order or state left by another test.

mustKnow.title: Test behavior, not implementation
mustKnow.body: Test inputs and observable results through a public interface rather than the order or count of internal method calls. Tests tied to implementation details break during refactoring even when behavior stays correct. This can discourage refactoring or lead teams to weaken tests until they no longer detect bugs. Exporting internal functions solely to test them is a common warning sign.

mustKnow.title: Test doubles: mocks, stubs, and fakes
mustKnow.body: Test doubles replace dependencies that are slow or hard to control, such as networks, clocks, or payment gateways. A stub returns predefined values; a fake is a simplified working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. A mock verifies calls and their arguments, which is useful for side effects that are not visible in the return value, such as sending email. In Jest, all three are often created with jest.fn() and called mocks, but distinguishing their roles helps you choose whether to assert results or interactions.

mustKnow.title: Boundary values: bugs at the edges
mustKnow.body: Errors such as using > instead of >= or an off-by-one loop often appear only at a boundary, so testing values in the middle can miss them. Divide inputs into equivalence partitions and test values immediately on both sides of each boundary. For free shipping from 500 onward, test 499 and 500 rather than only 100 and 1000. Also consider zero, negative values, empty lists, empty strings, and null.

mustKnow.title: Linter, formatter and static analysis
mustKnow.body: Linters, type checkers, and formatters inspect code without running it. Tools such as ESLint, the TypeScript type checker, and Prettier handle recurring issues across the codebase, including unused variables, incompatible types, and—through typescript-eslint rules—promises that were not awaited, faster and more cheaply than separate tests for each case. Keep their results consistent in the editor, pre-commit checks, and CI so reviews focus on logic and design rather than style. These tools cannot establish whether business rules are correct, so they do not replace tests.

mustKnow.title: What coverage can and cannot tell you
mustKnow.body: Coverage shows which lines or branches ran during tests, helping you find untested code. It does not show whether the results were asserted: merely calling a function can increase coverage. A mandatory percentage can encourage meaningless tests. Use coverage, especially branch coverage, to find blind spots rather than to prove test quality.

mustKnow.title: Flaky tests: inconsistent results
mustKnow.body: A flaky test passes and fails without a code change, often because it depends on real time, fixed sleeps, shared state, test order, or an external network. Repeated reruns can train a team to ignore failures that indicate real bugs. Fix the cause by controlling the clock, using fake timers, or isolating each test’s state. If an immediate fix is not possible, quarantine the test with tracked follow-up work instead of relying permanently on retries.

mustKnow.title: TDD: Red, Green, Refactor
mustKnow.body: Write a failing test for the next behavior (Red), write the smallest implementation that passes (Green), then improve the code while tests protect its behavior (Refactor). Observing the initial failure demonstrates that the test detects the missing behavior. If it passes immediately, either the behavior already exists or the test is not checking it correctly. TDD works well for clear logic with fast feedback; exploratory work or a rapidly changing UI may call for tests afterward.

mustKnow.title: Over-mocking: green tests, broken systems
mustKnow.body: Mocking every dependency, including your own classes, may verify only that code makes the calls you expected. A mock can return a result that the real dependency would never produce, leaving tests green despite invalid SQL or a renamed field. Warning signs include mock setup longer than the test and failures after every refactor. Prefer mocking boundaries you do not own, use fakes when practical, and add integration tests against real dependencies, for example a database started with Testcontainers.

mustKnow.title: Performance and load testing
mustKnow.body: Load testing measures behavior at expected traffic levels; stress testing pushes beyond them to find limits; soak testing runs for longer to expose issues such as memory leaks. Inspect high-percentile latency (p95 and p99) and error rates rather than averages that hide slow requests. Results are useful when the environment, data volume, and usage patterns resemble production. Common tools include k6, JMeter, Gatling, and Locust.

mustKnow.title: Contract testing and mutation testing
mustKnow.body: Contract testing checks that a consumer and provider can still communicate correctly. In consumer-driven testing, such as Pact, the consumer records its API expectations as a contract that the provider checks in CI, catching changed fields without E2E tests spanning every service. Mutation testing, such as StrykerJS for JavaScript or PIT for Java, makes small code changes—for example, replacing >= with >—and reruns tests; a surviving mutant usually means the tests do not check that behavior, except for equivalent mutants that no test can distinguish from the original. It measures test quality more directly than coverage but is slower, so teams often run it on changed code or periodically.

mustKnow.title: ISTQB’s seven testing principles
mustKnow.body: ISTQB gives seven testing principles: testing shows the presence, not the absence, of defects; exhaustive testing is impossible, so choose tests using techniques and risk; early testing saves time and money; defects cluster in a few components; tests wear out; testing is context-dependent; and meeting every requirement does not guarantee that a system meets user needs. Repeating unchanged tests detects fewer new defects, so refresh tests and data, and validate user needs as well as verifying requirements. Do not interpret “tests wear out” as saying repeated regression tests are useless: the syllabus explicitly recognizes their value in cases such as automated regression testing.

mustKnow.title: Test levels versus test types
mustKnow.body: A test level identifies where you test: ISTQB lists component (or unit), component integration, system, system integration, and acceptance testing. A test type identifies what you test: functional, non-functional (such as performance, security, or usability), black-box, or white-box testing. Each type can apply at any level; measuring a single function’s response time is a non-functional component test. Distinguish component integration, between components inside your system, from system integration, with another system or external service such as a payment gateway.

mustKnow.title: Confirmation testing and regression testing
mustKnow.body: After a bug fix, confirmation testing verifies that the original defect is fixed, for example by rerunning the previously failing case. Regression testing checks that the change, including a confirmed fix, has not broken the same component, other components, or connected systems. After fixing a coupon calculation, rerun the previously incorrect coupon case for confirmation, then run the full set of checkout and pricing tests for regression. Regression suites run frequently and keep growing, making them good candidates for automation in CI; use impact analysis to choose their scope.

mustKnow.title: Async tests: await or return the promise
mustKnow.body: Jest must know when asynchronous work finishes: return its promise or await it. Otherwise the test may finish before a promise resolves or rejects. Always await or return .resolves and .rejects assertions. With try/catch, ensure the test also fails if no rejection occurs, for example using expect.assertions(n) or storing the error and asserting outside the catch.

mustKnow.title: Setup, teardown, and isolated state
mustKnow.body: beforeEach and afterEach run around each test; beforeAll and afterAll run once for their file or describe block. Hooks inside describe apply to that block, and outer beforeEach hooks run before inner ones. A test that passes alone but fails with the suite often depends on state left by another test. Create or reset mutable data in beforeEach rather than sharing it at file scope or through beforeAll.

mustKnow.title: Defect reports: severity and priority
mustKnow.body: A defect report should let someone reproduce and fix a problem without follow-up questions. Include a concise title, the test object and environment, reproduction steps, expected and actual results, logs or screenshots, severity, priority, and status. In the ISTQB syllabus, severity describes the degree of impact on stakeholders or requirements, while priority describes the order of fixing defects; the two need not align. A distorted homepage logo before tomorrow’s press conference may have low functional impact but need an immediate fix.

mustKnow.title: Decision table and state transition testing
mustKnow.body: A decision table describes outcomes determined by combinations of conditions: rows hold conditions and actions, and columns hold rules. Coverage measures the proportion of feasible rules tested, helping reveal missing combinations or conflicting rules, but the number of rules grows quickly: three boolean conditions yield eight combinations. State transition testing suits systems whose behavior depends on state, such as orders; test cases are event sequences, and the syllabus describes all states, valid transitions, and all transitions coverage. The last also attempts invalid transitions; test them separately so one defect does not mask another.
mustKnow.code:
# Illustrative example: store discount rules
condition / rule      R1  R2  R3  R4
is_member             T   T   F   F
total >= 1000         T   F   T   F
----------------------------------
discount 15%          X
discount 5%               X   X
no discount                       X

mustKnow.title: Playwright: locators, auto-waiting, and assertions
mustKnow.body: Playwright automatically waits for an element to be ready before acting: a click checks that it uniquely matches, is visible, stable, unobstructed, and enabled. Prefer user-facing locators such as getByRole over selectors coupled to DOM structure. Use retrying web-first assertions such as await expect(locator).toBeVisible(); expect(await locator.isVisible()).toBe(true) checks only once and can be flaky. Keep each test independent of previous tests.

mustKnow.title: Snapshot testing: review the diff
mustKnow.body: Snapshot tests save serialized output in a text file and compare future output against it, making them useful for small, specific structures such as component output or error messages. Commit .snap files and review their diffs as part of the test. Control changing values such as time and random IDs, or use property matchers; Jest does not create new snapshots automatically in CI mode. Updating with jest -u without reading the diff turns the test into a rubber stamp for unintended changes.

mustKnow.title: Property-based testing with fast-check
mustKnow.body: Property-based testing defines relationships between input and output that must hold for all supported inputs. A library generates many inputs and shrinks a failing case toward the smallest counterexample it can find. Example properties include sorted output being nondecreasing with unchanged length, or decode(encode(x)) returning x. A general caution, not taken from the linked page: duplicating the implementation’s formula in a property can reproduce the same error and detect nothing.

mustKnow.title: Risk-based testing: prioritize by risk
mustKnow.body: When exhaustive testing is impossible, ISTQB recommends prioritizing by risk: the likelihood of a problem and its impact. Assess risk quantitatively by multiplying likelihood and impact, or qualitatively with a risk matrix. Use it to choose test levels, techniques, scope, and coverage depth. Newly written authentication code usually deserves more attention than renamed button labels; defect history also informs the assessment.

mustKnow.title: jest.mock hoisting and partial mocks
mustKnow.body: With babel-jest, jest.mock calls are hoisted before imports, so their factories cannot normally reference variables outside their scope. Jest permits names beginning with mock, but you must ensure those variables are initialized when needed. A factory that returns only some exports removes the rest; use jest.requireActual to preserve real exports and replace only selected ones. For different mocks in individual tests, use jest.doMock, which is not hoisted.

questions.prompt: Most of one service’s work is handling requests and reading or writing PostgreSQL. Its many unit tests mock every repository, but most production bugs involve invalid SQL or migrations that do not match the code. How should the team adjust its testing strategy?
options: Add more unit tests with mocked repositories to cover every query type.
Add integration tests using real PostgreSQL, for example in a container.
Add UI E2E tests for every possible case of every endpoint.
Require every PR to meet a minimum of 90% coverage in CI.
questions.explain: The bugs occur at the database boundary, which mocks cannot exercise. Integration tests are the lowest layer that can catch them, so give that layer more emphasis. More mocked unit tests can stay green despite invalid SQL, while E2E tests for every case would be unnecessarily slow and brittle.

questions.prompt: This test fails in CI under the vague name “order”. What is its main problem?
options: It has several expect calls; a unit test must always contain exactly one assertion.
It creates a real Order rather than a mock, so it cannot be a unit test.
It combines several behaviors, making a failure hard to diagnose.
It does not use beforeEach, making the test slow and hard to read.
questions.explain: Billing, coupons, and cancellation are checked under one name, so a failure requires inspecting the test, and later assertions never run. Split the behaviors into clearly named tests. Multiple assertions are fine when they check the same behavior.

questions.prompt: This test passes locally but sometimes fails on a busy CI machine. What addresses the cause?
options: Increase the sleep to 2000 ms to allow more time on slow CI machines.
Configure CI to retry failing tests three times before reporting results.
Have startReportJob return a promise; await it instead of using sleep.
Run this test last so other tests cannot compete with it for CPU time.
questions.explain: The test assumes the job finishes within 200 ms, which may fail on a busy CI machine. Wait for completion directly, or control time with fake timers. Longer sleeps make every run slower without removing the cause; retries hide it.

questions.prompt: You are using TDD to add a rule: “VIP members get a 10% discount.” The new test passes before you change any code. What should you do next?
options: Skip to refactoring because the test is already green.
Delete the test because a test that never failed is useless.
Implement the discount as planned and inspect the test afterward.
Check the test: it may miss the new rule, or the rule may exist.
questions.explain: The Red step demonstrates that a test detects missing behavior. An immediately passing test may have an incorrect assertion or setup, or the rule may already exist. Investigate before refactoring rather than trusting a test that has never shown the expected failure.

questions.prompt: The team refactors checkout to round to satang (hundredths of a baht) only once at the end. Every customer-visible total stays the same, but this test fails. What should change?
options: Change toHaveBeenCalledTimes to 1 to match the new implementation.
Assert checkout’s returned total instead of counting internal calls.
Revert the refactor because a failing test proves behavior changed.
Mock roundToSatang with a constant result to avoid testing rounding.
questions.explain: The test checks an internal calculation detail, so it breaks even though the result is unchanged. Changing the call count to 1 makes it pass but leaves it just as brittle for the next refactor. Assert the customer-visible result instead, for example expect(checkout(cart).total).toBe(...).

questions.prompt: A ticketing system offers student prices from ages 13 through 19, inclusive. Which set best tests the boundaries?
options: 15 alone, because the midpoint represents the entire range.
1, 15, 50, and 99 to spread tests across age groups.
12, 13, 19, and 20 to cover both sides of each boundary.
13 and 19 alone, because the requirements mention them.
questions.explain: Mistakes involving < versus <= or off-by-one errors occur at boundaries, so test just inside and just outside both ends of the range. Testing only 13 and 19 checks the inside values: an incorrect condition such as age <= 20 would still pass those tests.

questions.prompt: Most PR comments concern spacing, import order, and unused variables, leaving little review time for logic. What should the team change?
options: Write a detailed style guide and have reviewers manually enforce its rules.
Automate formatting and linting in the editor, pre-commit, and CI.
Add unit tests that check the coding style of each file.
Let one senior reviewer decide every question of coding style.
questions.explain: Automate checks that follow mechanical rules: tools apply them consistently and can often fix issues automatically. This frees reviewers to focus on logic and design. A manually enforced style guide still consumes review time and leaves room for different interpretations.

questions.prompt: This function has 100% coverage, but mutation testing reports that a mutant replacing >= with > survived. What does that mean?
options: No test distinguishes >= from >; add a case where total is exactly 500.
The tool is misconfigured because 100% coverage proves complete testing.
Change the code to > because the mutant passes the tests.
Add more test values between 100 and 1000 for denser coverage.
questions.explain: The changed code still passes, revealing that no test distinguishes behavior at exactly 500. Values away from that boundary cannot distinguish >= from >. Coverage records execution, not whether the boundary result was asserted.

questions.prompt: Orders calls a Users API maintained by another team. Users renames fullName to name and deploys; both teams’ tests pass, but Orders fails in production. What best prevents this?
options: Make Orders’ unit tests mock Users responses in greater detail.
Add Users unit tests until coverage reaches 100% before deployment.
Check Orders’ consumer contract in Users’ CI before deployment.
Run E2E tests across every service in shared staging before deployment.
questions.explain: The Orders mock encodes that team’s assumptions and stays green after Users changes the response. Contract tests check the consumer’s expectations in the provider’s CI before deployment. Cross-service E2E tests can also catch this, but are slower, more brittle, and depend on shared staging.

questions.prompt: A product-search API meets its latency target with an average of 120 ms in a load test, but some users report very slow searches. What should the team inspect next?
options: Inspect p95 and p99 latency alongside the error rate under the same load.
Rerun the load test with fewer simulated users to make results more stable.
Inspect the median because it is less sensitive to outliers than the mean.
Accept the result; users reporting delays probably have slow connections.
questions.explain: Both the mean and median can hide very slow requests. If p99 is several seconds, roughly one in a hundred requests waits that long despite a good average, so inspect high percentiles alongside the error rate. Reducing the load may improve the numbers but no longer reflects real conditions.

questions.prompt: A suite of 600 automated regression tests has passed every night for six months, yet new bugs in frequently changed features keep reaching users. Which conclusion best fits the testing principles?
options: The suite detects fewer new defects; update tests and data for changed features.
Nightly passes prove no defects remain; escaped bugs must be requirement changes.
Stop automated regression entirely because repeating tests has no value.
Run the unchanged suite several times a night so it detects more bugs.
questions.explain: The “tests wear out” principle calls for updating tests and data or adding cases when unchanged tests detect fewer new defects. Repeated tests still have value, including automated regression, so do not abandon them. Running the same checks more often does not expand what they test.

questions.prompt: Several months of defect history show most customer-reported bugs in one tax module. Testing time before release is limited. How should the team allocate it?
options: Divide time equally across modules to be fair and leave none neglected.
Give the tax module extra testing time because defects cluster there.
Skip the tax module; its many bugs mean testing it would never finish.
Test only newly written modules because older modules have already been used.
questions.explain: The “defects cluster” principle says that a few components often contain most defects. Historical defect data helps prioritize testing by risk, so focus extra effort on the tax module. Equal allocation ignores risk, while skipping the module because it has many bugs reverses the principle.

questions.prompt: The team tests every requirement in the specification and fixes every defect found. After release, users say the workflow does not match their work and is too difficult to use. Which concept explains this?
options: Pesticide paradox: repeated tests no longer detect new defects.
Exhaustive testing is impossible: not every input and path can be tested.
Absence-of-defects fallacy: meeting requirements may not meet user needs.
Defect clustering: all bugs are concentrated in one system module.
questions.explain: Verification checks conformance to the specification, but does not establish that the specification meets real user needs. Add validation, such as trials with actual users or acceptance testing. The pesticide paradox concerns the effectiveness of repeated tests, which is not the issue here.

questions.prompt: The team tests an external provider’s payment gateway in its sandbox to check that requests and responses match the agreed contract. Which ISTQB test level is this?
options: Component testing: it directly tests our payment module in isolation.
Component integration testing: it checks an interface between two code components.
Acceptance testing: it uses data resembling real transactions.
System integration testing: it checks an interface with an external service.
questions.explain: System integration testing checks interfaces between the system under test and other systems or external services, ideally in an environment resembling production. Component integration, the most tempting alternative, concerns interfaces between components within the same system.

questions.prompt: A developer fixes incorrect totals caused by overlapping coupons. QA reruns the previously failing case and it passes. What should happen before closing the ticket?
options: Run regression tests for affected areas, such as pricing and checkout.
Close the ticket because passing confirmation testing proves the fix is complete.
Rerun the same case dozens of times to rule out flakiness before closing.
Test only the discount screen because that is where users see the result.
questions.explain: Confirmation testing establishes only that the original defect is fixed. Regression testing checks for adverse effects elsewhere and is still needed after a fix passes confirmation. Closing the ticket immediately skips that check.

questions.prompt: Which e-commerce defect is best described as low severity but high priority?
options: Credit-card checkout crashes throughout a flash sale, preventing purchases.
An unused legacy report export crashes the whole system when its button is clicked.
Tomorrow’s campaign page misspells the brand name, but the system works normally.
The language button is two pixels out of place on a few phones, with little notice.
questions.explain: Severity measures impact, while priority reflects urgency. A misspelled brand name on tomorrow’s campaign page has low functional impact but needs an immediate fix. A payment failure during a sale is high in both; a rarely used feature that crashes the whole system can have high severity but lower priority.

questions.prompt: Shipping rules depend on three boolean conditions: membership, reaching a spending threshold, and having a free-shipping coupon. Outcomes depend on their combinations. How many rules are in the full unreduced decision table, and how is coverage measured?
options: 3 rules, one per condition; coverage is the proportion of conditions tested.
8 rules; coverage is the proportion of feasible rules tested.
6 rules, two per condition; coverage is measured by the total test count.
9 rules, three conditions times three values; coverage is measured by executed lines.
questions.explain: Three true/false conditions yield 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. Decision table coverage is the number of feasible columns tested divided by the total number of feasible columns. Adding the values or assigning one rule per condition misses the fact that outcomes depend on combinations.

questions.prompt: An order can be Created, Paid, Shipped, or Closed, and cancellation is allowed only before shipping. The team targets “all transitions coverage”. After testing every valid transition, what else is required?
options: Nothing: visiting every state already gives complete coverage.
Nothing: every valid transition already covers all transitions.
Attempt all invalid transitions in one test to save time.
Attempt invalid transitions, such as cancellation after shipping, in separate tests.
questions.explain: All transitions coverage includes valid transitions and attempts at invalid ones. Test invalid transitions separately to avoid defect masking, where one defect prevents another from being detected. Combining them risks missing defects; valid transitions coverage alone is a weaker target.

questions.prompt: Async getUser should reject with "not found", but a bug makes it resolve to null. The test below still passes. How should the test detect this?
options: Await expect(e.message) inside catch so it waits for the result.
Use expect(() => getUser(999)).toThrow("not found") without await.
Use await expect(getUser(999)).rejects.toThrow("not found").
Increase the timeout to give catch more time to run.
questions.explain: If getUser resolves, the catch block never runs, so no assertion executes and the test passes without checking the result. Use an awaited .rejects assertion, which fails on fulfillment, or expect.assertions(1). Awaiting inside catch cannot make that block run, and a synchronous toThrow assertion cannot detect an async rejection, so it would fail even after the implementation is fixed.

questions.prompt: The second test below passes with test.only but fails when both tests run together. What is the cause and fix?
options: Jest always randomizes tests; configure file-order execution.
The count function is wrong on repeated calls; edit only production code.
Create the cart once in beforeAll to make tests faster.
The shared cart retains changes; create a fresh cart in beforeEach.
questions.explain: The first test mutates a file-level cart, so the second sees leftover contents only when run together. Creating a new cart in beforeEach gives each test the same starting state. beforeAll preserves shared state, and Jest does not randomize tests in an ordinary file by default.

questions.prompt: A component change makes snapshot tests fail in 14 files. A developer runs jest -u and commits every update without reading it. What is the problem?
options: No problem: snapshots come from real code, so they are always correct.
Updating blindly accepts unintended changes; review the diff first.
Do not commit .snap files because Jest generates them automatically.
Delete every snapshot test and replace each one with a toBe assertion.
questions.explain: Snapshot files are part of the tests and need code review. Updating them without reading the diff can accept unintended behavior. Commit .snap files to version control, as Jest recommends, after reviewing the changes.

questions.prompt: A developer adds a toMatchSnapshot test, sees it pass locally, but forgets to commit the .snap file. CI runs Jest with --ci. What happens?
options: The test passes and CI automatically writes a new .snap file.
The test is skipped until a .snap file appears in the repository.
The test fails; CI will not create snapshots. Commit the .snap file.
The test passes with a warning that its snapshot has not been saved.
questions.explain: In --ci mode, Jest fails a new snapshot rather than writing it unless --updateSnapshot is explicitly supplied. This prevents unreviewed snapshots from being accepted automatically. Commit the reviewed .snap file.

questions.prompt: Jest reports that the module factory in this jest.mock() call cannot reference an out-of-scope variable. Which explanation and fix are correct?
questions.code:
const fakeMailer = { send: jest.fn() };
jest.mock('./mailer', () => fakeMailer);
options: jest.fn cannot be used inside a factory; write a normal function instead.
Move jest.mock after require because Jest always follows source order.
Use jest.doMock whenever a factory references an external variable; there is no alternative.
jest.mock is hoisted; use a mock-prefixed variable initialized before the factory needs it.
questions.explain: Hoisting moves jest.mock ahead of imports, so Jest restricts out-of-scope variables that may not yet be initialized. Names starting with mock are allowed, but you must still initialize them in time. Non-hoisted jest.doMock is another option, not the only one.

questions.prompt: This E2E test is flaky because the “Saved” toast appears about 300 ms after the click. What fixes the cause?
options: Use await expect(page.getByText("Saved")).toBeVisible().
Add await page.waitForTimeout(2000) before checking the toast.
Set the runner’s retries to 3 so it reruns the whole test on failure.
Use a more specific CSS selector for the toast to improve stability.
questions.explain: isVisible() checks once and returns immediately without waiting. A web-first assertion such as toBeVisible() retries until the condition holds or the timeout expires. A fixed delay still guesses when the toast will appear, and runner retries hide the problem.

questions.prompt: A designer renames CSS classes across the site. Almost every E2E test fails although the pages work as before. Most locators look like div.card > button.btn-x1:nth-child(2). How should they change?
options: Forbid future class renaming because tests depend on those names.
Use getByRole with the button’s name, or an agreed test ID.
Use full XPath selectors from the root because they are more precise.
Halve the E2E suite to reduce maintenance after refactoring.
questions.explain: Locators tied to DOM structure or CSS classes break when markup changes even if behavior stays the same. Playwright recommends user-facing locators such as roles, or explicit test IDs as a shared contract. Long XPath selectors would be even more brittle.

questions.prompt: The “Edit Profile” E2E test depends on a previous “Login” test leaving a session behind. It fails alone or in parallel. What enables independent tests and clear failure diagnosis?
options: Always run the login test first and disable parallel execution.
Combine all steps into one long test to avoid dependencies between tests.
Retry the profile test in case the session becomes available in time.
Log in during each test’s beforeEach, independently of other tests.
questions.explain: Give each test its own storage, cookies, and data so it runs independently, produces repeatable results, and is easier to debug. Enforcing an order treats the symptom and lets one failure cascade into others. A single long test avoids dependencies between tests but combines behaviors, making the failing feature harder to identify.

questions.prompt: This property test passes even when sortNumbers returns an unsorted array. Which property detects the bug?
options: Check that adjacent elements are in nondecreasing order.
Generate ten times as many random inputs to increase coverage.
Check that the result is always an array, regardless of the input.
Check that sortNumbers never throws for any generated input.
questions.explain: The existing property checks only length, which unsorted output can preserve. Assert that adjacent elements are nondecreasing. More random inputs cannot compensate for a property that never checks ordering; checking only the array type or absence of errors is too weak.

questions.prompt: Two testing days remain before release. There is a completely new payment module, an About page with only text changes, and an internal report used once a month. What should risk-based testing prioritize?
options: Start with the easiest part to test to raise coverage as quickly as possible.
Start with payments: both the likelihood of defects and their impact are high.
Test in application menu order to ensure no section is missed.
Give every area equal testing time to keep the allocation fair.
questions.explain: Risk depends on likelihood and impact. Newly written payment code has a high likelihood of defects, and errors involving money have a high impact, so it deserves the highest priority and the most testing time. Starting with easy areas improves coverage numbers without addressing the greatest risk.

questions.prompt: The function below has only one test, discount(1000, true). What does coverage show, and what is needed for complete branch coverage?
options: 100% statement and branch coverage because every line runs.
50% statement and branch coverage; add tests for both cases.
100% statements, incomplete branches; test isMember=false.
Incomplete statement coverage; add a test reaching the return.
questions.explain: The single test executes every statement, giving 100% statement coverage, but never takes the false branch of the if, leaving branch coverage at 50%. Add a case with isMember set to false. Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, but statement coverage does not imply full branch coverage.

questions.prompt: A new file-import feature has sparse requirements and one day until delivery. Which additional testing approach is most useful?
options: Use session-based exploratory testing with a charter and a time box.
Wait for complete specifications to avoid testing the wrong behavior.
Document detailed test cases for every scenario before executing any tests.
Use only unit tests because they are fast and require no tester judgment.
questions.explain: Exploratory testing combines designing, running, and evaluating tests with learning about the system. It is useful when specifications are sparse or time is limited. A session charter and time box provide structure; waiting for complete specifications could leave no time to test.

exercises.title: Test shipping-fee boundary values
exercises.prompt: shippingFee(total) charges 50 baht, gives free shipping for totals of at least 500 baht, and throws for negative totals. Write at least four Jest unit tests, each checking one behavior by calling shippingFee directly. Cover both sides of 500, zero, and a negative total.
hints: Separate totals below 500, totals from 500 onward, and negative totals; choose boundary values for each group.
Use 499 and 500 for the free-shipping boundary, and -1 and 0 for the negative-total boundary.
Wrap throwing calls in a function: expect(() => shippingFee(-1)).toThrow(). Calling expect(shippingFee(-1)) throws before expect can run.

checks.label: Include at least four test cases
Test exactly 500
Test 499, just below the boundary
Test a total of zero
Assert the error with toThrow
Wrap throwing calls in a function passed to expect
Assert the returned value with toBe or toEqual

exercises.title: Test async welcome emails with stubs and mocks
exercises.prompt: sendWelcome receives repo (user lookup) and mailer (email sending) as dependencies. Write at least three async Jest tests: a user with an email returns sent: true and calls mailer.send with that email; a user without an email returns sent: false and does not call mailer.send; and a missing user rejects with "user not found". Use jest.fn() for stubs and mocks instead of real dependencies, and await every promise.
hints: Pass fresh dependency objects into the function rather than mocking the whole module. Reset them in beforeEach to avoid state leaking between tests.
repo.findById and mailer.send are async. Use jest.fn().mockResolvedValue(...) and await sendWelcome(...) in an async test.

Check no email with expect(mailer.send).not.toHaveBeenCalled(); check a missing user with await expect(sendWelcome(...)).rejects.toThrow("user not found"). Without await, the test can finish before the assertion.

checks.label: Include at least three test cases
Await async tests and stub the repository with a promise-returning function
Check sent: true with an email and sent: false without one
Verify mailer.send receives the user’s email
Verify no mailer.send call when email is absent
Assert a missing-user rejection with rejects, assertion counts, or a check outside catch
Await or return rejects/resolves assertions

exercises.title: Test delayed retries with fake timers
exercises.prompt: retry calls fn once, then retries up to retries times after failures, waiting delayMs between attempts. If every attempt fails, it rejects with the last error. Replace slow real-clock tests with fake timers: verify success on the third call after two failures; verify that fn is called once before delayMs and again when the delay expires; and verify rejection with the final error when all attempts fail. Restore real timers after each test.
hints: Enable fake timers in beforeEach with jest.useFakeTimers(), and restore real timers in afterEach with jest.useRealTimers().
Use await jest.advanceTimersByTimeAsync(ms) so promise callbacks run during time advancement. The synchronous version does not let pending promises continue in the same way.
Attach const assertion = expect(retry(...)).rejects.toThrow("...") before advancing time, then await assertion at the end. Attaching it later can leave the rejection unhandled.

checks.label: Enable fake timers with jest.useFakeTimers()
Advance timers asynchronously with advanceTimersByTimeAsync or runAllTimersAsync
Restore real timers in afterEach (or afterAll)
Verify one fn call before the delay ends
Verify three fn calls
Assert rejection when all attempts fail
Avoid real-time setTimeout waits in tests

cheatsheet: Test each risk at the lowest layer that can detect it; emphasize integration tests for code connecting to databases or services.
AAA means Arrange, Act, Assert; each test checks one behavior, but may use several assertions for the same result.
A stub returns predefined values; a fake is a simplified working implementation; a mock verifies calls and arguments.
Test immediately on both sides of a boundary: free shipping from 500 needs 499 and 500 to catch incorrect use of > versus >=.
A test level identifies where you test; a test type identifies what you test, and each type can apply at any level.
Confirmation testing checks that the original defect is fixed; regression testing checks that the change has not broken other areas.
In Jest, await or return promises, including .resolves and .rejects assertions, or the test may finish before checking the result.
Coverage shows execution, not whether results were asserted; use branch coverage to find blind spots, not to prove test quality.
Severity measures impact; priority describes the order of fixing defects, so the two need not align.
Prioritize tests by risk: assess it quantitatively with likelihood × impact, or qualitatively with a risk matrix.
